hero.title: Single-ply and low-slope roofs
hero.lead: For shops, warehouses, offices and light-industrial buildings. Built to drain, detailed at every curb and edge, and scheduled around the business underneath.

image.alt: White single-ply membrane roof with rooftop HVAC units on curbs, seen from above

buildings.title: Shops, warehouses and light industrial
buildings.body:
Commercial roofing, for us, means the low-slope roofs on shop buildings, warehouses, flex space with offices up front and a roll-up door out back, small office buildings and strip retail.

These roofs have more going on than you'd guess from the parking lot: rooftop units, exhaust fans, skylights, gas lines, conduit, and years of repairs by whoever was closest. We start by walking all of it and writing down what's there.

workTypes.title: Replacement
workTypes.body: Tear-off to the deck, or where the existing roof is dry and sound and the code allows it, a recover over it. We'll tell you which one your building qualifies for.

workTypes.title: Repair
workTypes.body: Leaks at curbs, seams, drains, walls and edges, and wind damage after a storm. Found at the source, fixed in the same membrane.

workTypes.title: Reports and maintenance
workTypes.body: A written condition report when you need to plan or budget, and scheduled visits to keep drains open and details tight.

image.alt: Aerial view of a long light-industrial building and a smaller shop building, both with pale low-slope roofs and rooftop units, surrounded by trees

buildings.caption: Light-industrial buildings like these carry acres of low-slope roof, broken up by units, vents and expansion joints. Every one of those is a detail to get right.

singlePly.title: Single-ply membrane: TPO and PVC
singlePly.body:
Most low-slope commercial roofs we replace get a single-ply membrane: one layer of reinforced thermoplastic sheet over insulation and cover board, with every seam fused shut.

Heat-welded seams

The sheets overlap at the seams, and a hot-air welder melts the two layers together into one piece. There's no tape or glue in the lap to dry out over the years. After welding, we run a probe along every seam to find any spot that didn't fuse, and fix it before we leave the roof.

TPO or PVC

Both are white, both are heat-welded, and from the ground they look the same. TPO (thermoplastic polyolefin) is the usual choice for re-roofing shops, warehouses and offices. It's economical and holds up well in general use. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) costs more, but it stands up better to grease, oils and many chemicals, which is why it's the usual pick around a restaurant's kitchen exhaust or where a process vents onto the roof. We'll tell you which one your building needs, and why.

A white surface

A white membrane reflects most of the summer sun instead of soaking it up, so the roof and the space below run cooler in July and August, and the membrane sees less heat stress. In our climate the bigger issue is dirt: under firs and maples, a white roof picks up a gray-green film that dulls it. A rinse on maintenance visits keeps it reflecting.

attachment.label: Two ways to hold it down

items.title: Mechanically attached
items.body: Insulation and membrane are screwed to the deck through steel plates. The fasteners sit in the seam laps and the next sheet is welded over them. Quick to install, less fussy about weather, and common on steel decks.

items.title: Fully adhered
items.body: The membrane is glued to the cover board across its whole area. No flutter in wind, a smoother finish, and a good fit for roofs crowded with penetrations. Adhesives need a dry surface and mild temperatures, so the weather matters more.

attachment.note: Which one fits depends on the deck, the building's height and exposure, and the wind design for the site. We spec it for your building, not from a catalog.

compare.title: How single-ply compares
compare.intro: You'll find all five of these on low-slope roofs around the metro, and it helps to know which one you have. The single-ply roofs we install are TPO and PVC.

systems.name: TPO
systems.note: The common choice for re-roofing low-slope commercial buildings. Reflective surface.

systems.name: PVC
systems.note: Holds up better than TPO to grease, oils and many chemicals. Costs more.

systems.name: EPDM
systems.what: Synthetic rubber single-ply sheet, usually black
systems.note: Long track record and flexible in the cold. The laps are the usual weak point as it ages.

systems.name: Modified bitumen
systems.what: Asphalt sheets with polymer modifiers, in two or more plies
systems.note: Tough under foot traffic. Torch-applied work carries a fire risk on an occupied building.

systems.name: Built-up (tar & gravel)
systems.what: Alternating layers of felt and hot asphalt, often with gravel on top
systems.note: Common on older buildings. Heavy, and the gravel hides the membrane, so leaks are hard to trace.

lowSlope.title: Low-slope roofs: drainage is everything
lowSlope.intro: A low-slope roof isn't flat, or shouldn't be. Every square foot needs somewhere to send water, and in a Portland winter the water keeps coming for weeks. If it's still standing 48 hours after the rain stops, the roof isn't draining.
lowSlope.swipeHint: Swipe the drawing to see the whole section.
lowSlope.caption: Section through a low-slope roof, not to scale. Water runs down the taper to the drain; the overflow in the wall only works if the drain doesn't.

keys.title: Tapered insulation
keys.body: Insulation boards cut with a built-in slope, laid so every part of the roof falls toward a drain. On a replacement, it's how a roof that ponds gets fixed for good instead of patched around. The usual target for a new membrane roof is at least a quarter inch of fall per foot.

keys.title: Drains
keys.body: Interior drains sit at the low points, with the membrane clamped into the drain bowl under a ring. The strainer on top keeps fir needles and leaves out of the pipe. A slow drain is a roof that ponds.

keys.title: Scuppers & overflows
keys.body: An overflow scupper or secondary drain sits a little above the primary one, so if the main drain clogs, water leaves through the wall instead of piling weight on the roof. Water coming out of an overflow means the primary drain needs attention.

keys.title: Crickets
keys.body: A small ridge built on the uphill side of a curb, chimney or wide unit. It splits the water and sends it around. Without one, water sits against the curb and eventually finds the flashing.

keys.title: Parapets & edges
keys.body: Membrane runs up the inside of the wall under a termination bar, and metal coping caps the top with a slight pitch back onto the roof. At an open edge, the edge metal is what wind grabs first, so it's fastened to hold.

details.title: Why leaks start at the details
details.body: The field of a membrane roof is one continuous sheet, and the seams are welded and probed. Leaks tend to start where the sheet stops: at a curb, a pipe, a drain, a wall or an edge. That's where we spend the time on a new roof, and where we look first on a repair.

details.title: Curbs, units, pipes, walls and edges
details.intro: Every hole in a membrane roof is a detail somebody has to get right. These are the ones we spend the time on.

image.alt: Low-slope roof with a large rooftop unit on a curb, a brick parapet with metal coping, a ladder, a roof drain with staining around it and two small condensers

details.caption: A unit on its curb, a parapet with metal coping, and a drain with a stain around it where water sits after rain. Four details in one corner of one roof.

items.title: Curbs & rooftop units
items.body: Membrane runs up the curb and is sealed under the unit's flange or counterflashed, high enough that ponded or drifting water can't reach the top. Curbs that are too short get raised during a replacement, coordinated with your HVAC contractor.

items.title: Pipes, conduit & gas lines
items.body: Round penetrations get prefabricated or field-welded boots, clamped at the top. Old pitch pans full of sealant need topping up forever, so we replace them with boots wherever the penetration allows. Gas lines and conduit sit on supports, not on the membrane.

items.title: Parapets & coping
items.body: Membrane goes up the inside of the wall and, where the detail calls for it, over the top and under metal coping with sealed or cleated joints. A lot of leaks that seem to come from nowhere start at a loose coping joint: wind-driven rain gets in and runs down inside the wall.

items.title: Edge metal
items.body: On a roof without parapets, the edge is where wind starts peeling. Edge metal is fastened on a tight pattern and the membrane is stripped in over it. Where the roof drains to a gutter, the gutter is sized for the area it serves.

items.title: Drains
items.body: Corroded drain bodies get replaced or fitted with retrofit inserts. The membrane clamps into the bowl, and the strainer goes back on before we leave.

items.title: Skylights & hatches
items.body: Curb-mounted skylights and roof hatches are flashed like any other curb. Old plastic domes crack and leak at the frame, and they are much easier to replace during a reroof than after it.

occupied.title: Working around a business that's open
occupied.intro: The building has to keep working while its roof is replaced. That takes a plan the manager, the tenants and the crew all know before the first sheet comes up.

steps.title: Walk it with whoever runs the building
steps.body: Access, hours, deliveries, loading docks, tenants with sensitive work below, equipment that can't lose power. Staging and the order of work are planned around what you tell us.

steps.title: Schedule the loud parts
steps.body: Tear-off and fastening are loud and shake the deck. We agree when those happen so tenants can be told which days. Early starts or weekend work are possible where the city and the neighbors allow it.

steps.title: Stage it and keep it safe
steps.body: Material goes up by lift or crane at agreed times and sits where the structure can take it. The ground below the work is taped or fenced off, entrances stay open, and edges get warning lines or guardrails.

steps.title: Dry every night
steps.body: We only tear off what we can close the same day. At the end of each shift the new roof is tied in to the old with a temporary seal and the drains are left open. If rain is on the way, less comes off.

steps.title: Protect what's underneath
steps.body: Tear-off shakes dust and debris loose above ceilings. Where the space below holds stock, equipment or an office, we'll say so ahead of time so it can be covered or moved.

steps.title: Close it out
steps.body: We walk the finished roof with you, clear the drains, and hand over photos of the work, including the details that end up covered.

maintenance.title: Condition reports and upkeep
maintenance.intro: A roof assessment tells you what you have, how long it's likely to last, and what to spend on first. It's the right start if you're buying a building, setting next year's budget, or tired of paying for the same leak twice.

report.title: What a condition report covers
items: A roof plan with areas, drains, units and penetrations marked
The roof system, number of layers and approximate age, where it can be told
Seams, flashings, curbs, edges and drains, each with photos
Ponding areas and where the drainage is falling short
Wet insulation, where a moisture reading or a small core cut points to it (cores are patched the same day)
A ranked list: fix now, fix this year, plan for

visit.title: What a maintenance visit covers
items: Clear drains, strainers, scuppers and gutters
Remove fir needles, leaves, moss and debris, especially at the low points
Probe seams and check flashings at curbs and penetrations
Check sealant at terminations, counterflashing and pitch pans
Check coping and edge metal for loose joints
Note new penetrations cut by other trades since the last visit
Photos and a short written summary

maintenance.timing: Twice a year suits most commercial roofs here: in the fall, before the rain settles in and the needles drop, and in spring, after the winter has done its worst.
maintenance.storms: After an east wind, an ice storm or a hard blow, it's worth a look at the edges, coping and seams even if nothing is leaking yet. Wind damage at an edge usually leaks later, not the same night.

quote.title: What helps us quote it
quote.intro: None of this is required to get us out there. Whatever you can pull together means a shorter site visit and a sharper number.
quote.label: Before the site visit

items.title: Drawings, if you have them
items.body: Roof plans, as-builts or a previous roofing spec. Not required: if nothing's on file, we measure.

items.title: Roof access
items.body: How we get up: an interior hatch, a fixed ladder, or a lift from outside. Keys, codes, and who to call on site.

items.title: Age and history
items.body: When the roof went on, if anyone knows, and what's happened since: repairs, a recover, new units or new penetrations.

items.title: Known leak spots
items.body: Where it leaks and when: steady rain, wind-driven rain from the south, or only in a big storm. Photos of ceiling stains help.

items.title: How the building runs
items.body: Hours, tenants, deliveries, and anything under the roof that can't get wet or dusty.

closingCta.label: Commercial estimate
closingCta.title: Get the roof walked
closingCta.body: Tell us about the building and what the roof is doing. We'll walk it, look hard at the details, and give you a written, itemized estimate.
